_what_this_is: EVERY state the two update surfaces can be in, and what each one must say.
ONE TABLE, THREE READERS. The briefing line (framework/frontdoor/run_briefing,
_update_notice, pytest), the resolver the card is fed by
(cabinet/scripts/lib/update_bundle.resolve_update_surface, which is what
`cabinet-update.sh status --json` reports, pytest) and the home card itself
(cabinet/dashboard/src/lib/updates, updateHeadline + refusalToShow + the Apply
gate, vitest). Every row is driven through all three: the pytest half writes the
row's state document, its marker and its ledger to disk and runs the real
readers over them; the vitest half builds the status object `status --json`
reports for that row and runs the card over it.
DERIVED FROM THE CONTRACT (A5.17, rules 1-8), never from either
implementation. A row where the code disagrees is a defect in the CODE.
WHY AN EXHAUSTIVE TABLE AND NOT MORE ARMS. Five review rounds each found one
more adjacent state in these same readers: a refusal that outlived the bundle
it was about (round 1), a refusal that spoke over a running apply (round 2), a
refusal that outlived the apply that overtook it (round 3), a whole SECOND
refusal channel none of the rules had been applied to (round 4), and a resolver
whose currency was GLOBAL rather than per bundle (round 5). Every arm written
for each of them was aimed at the state that already worked. A product does not
have to be thought of.
WHY THESE SIX AXES. Round 4's defect lived where the 240-row table did not
look: every row ran on an EMPTY ledger. Round 5's lived where the 1440-row
table did not look: every row carried at most ONE receipt about the refused
bundle, so "the newest refusal about B" and "the newest refusal anywhere" were
indistinguishable, and the shape `refuse_busy` writes on EVERY lock contention
-- a verdict about B followed by a note about no bundle at all -- was not
representable at any point in the product. A completeness claim that holds an
input's DEPTH constant is a green hole, not a covered one. The ledger about B
is therefore an axis of SEQUENCES, and what the ledger says about anything else
is an axis of its own.
THE AXES (5 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 5 x 2 = 5250 rows, the whole product, nothing
skipped, no exclusions):
phase (5)          idle | refused | applying | applied | rolled_back
-- the state document's own last event. `applied` names B
as `to_sha`; `rolled_back` names B as `from_sha`, which is
the shape the updater writes (A5.17.4).
waiting (3)        nothing | B (the bundle the state axes are about) | E
(another bundle entirely). What is waiting is what the
surfaces are asked about, so it is the axis that decides
which bundle `current()` is called on.
state-about-B (5)  none | marker `locked` | marker `digest` | legacy
`last_refusal` verdict | legacy `last_refusal` busy.
Five because the durable store (a per-bundle marker) and
the legacy mirror are different channels with different
admission rules, and because a marker with PATHS and one
without decide the Apply button differently.
ledger-about-B (7) none | V | V then applied(B) | V then rolled_back(from B) |
V then busy(B) | V then V' (a newer digest verdict) |
applied(B) then V. Seven because two is the depth at which
"current about B" stops being "newest anywhere", and
because each of the four things that can follow a verdict
-- an apply, a rollback, a timing note, a second verdict --
is a different rule, plus the order-reversed case.
newest-not-about-B (5)
none | busy with an EMPTY sha | busy about E | a verdict
about E | applied E. Five because a record about another
bundle must never answer, suppress or blank a question
about this one -- and because when E is what is waiting,
the verdict about E is the one that must speak. Always the
NEWEST record in the ledger, which is the position the
round-5 defect turned on.
ledger_error (2)   absent | set (A5.16: the ledger FAILED, not a version
behind).
NO ROW IS EXCLUDED and none is skipped or xfailed. Combinations no writer
produces today -- a marker about B while the ledger's verdict about B is newer,
a `phase: refused` document with no refusal record in it -- are KEPT and
pinned: a state file can be truncated, hand-edited or written by an older
updater copy, a ledger can be restored from a backup, and what a reader does at
the degenerate end is exactly what five rounds of hand-written arms never
asked. The completeness arm rebuilds the id set from the DECLARED axes, so a
REMOVED row fails it, not only a changed one.
WHAT IS HELD OUTSIDE THE PRODUCT, and why that is not a hole. Four inputs are
claimed to be INDEPENDENT of the resolution rather than untested: a marker
about E, `last_busy` in any value, `event_fallback` on or off, and the POSITION
of the ledger's records (A5.17.3 -- only times are compared). Each is an
INVARIANCE arm over at least fifty sampled rows: the input is varied on a row
already in this table and the answer must not move. That is a stronger
statement than a product axis would make, and it is what keeps the product at
5250 rows instead of 90,000.
SEEDS ARE HOISTED PER AXIS VALUE. `ledger_seeds` and `other_seeds` carry the
events to emit, `markers` the marker file to write, `legacy` the state record,
`phase_state` the document's own event; a row is its axes plus what the
contract says must come out. Every seeded event carries `recorded_at` -- the
record's OWN time (A5.17.3), which is what the resolution orders by. The
ledger's insertion time is deliberately NOT usable: a record held for an older
emitter is replayed by the next apply and inserted days late.
THE TIMES, and why each axis sits where it does on the clock:
10:00:00  the ledger sequence's first event
10:00:05  the state document's own applied/rolled_back event
10:00:10  the state channel's verdict about B (marker or legacy)
10:00:20  the ledger sequence's second event
10:00:30  the newest ledger record NOT about B
So every pair of channels is ordered both ways somewhere in the product: the
state verdict is newer than the ledger's first record and older than its
second, and the state document's own event is older than the state verdict and
newer than the ledger's first.
WHAT EACH ROW CARRIES. `resolved` is what BOTH resolvers must produce -- the
record, the channel it came from, and the rollback-about-the-waiting-bundle
fact -- and it is the card's whole input. `expect` carries the exact SENTENCE
for each surface, whether the refusal sub-surface speaks, whether the Apply
button is live, and which channel answered. The sentences differ between the
surfaces in three declared places and only three: the applying sentence, the
rolled-back-state sentence, and where the ledger fault sits (the briefing has
ONE line and spends it on a fault above the waiting bundle; the card has room
to show the fault beside whatever it says, so it takes the headline only when
nothing else has one). `refusal_speaks` and `apply_live` are ONE property each,
consumed by both suites, so the sub-surfaces cannot disagree by construction.
A sentence or a flag changed here reds BOTH suites.
